cases.n: Argentina — junta's 'systematic plan' to appropriate babies (2012 verdict)
cases.place: Buenos Aires (ESMA naval school and other clandestine detention centres)
cases.who: Argentine military junta; armed forces and security forces; ESMA
cases.cover: Children's original identities were hidden and they were registered as the biological children of military families and regime allies.
cases.d: On 5 July 2012 Federal Oral Criminal Tribunal No. 6 of Buenos Aires found that the military junta had run a systematic plan to abduct children born to detained or disappeared mothers, between 1976 and 1983. Former dictator Jorge Videla was sentenced to 50 years and the last dictator, Reynaldo Bignone, to 15 years; nine other defendants received 15 to 40 years (MercoPress). The trial covered about 31–35 abductions. The tribunal convicted Bignone of crimes against humanity for implementing the plan.
cases.cite: Tribunal Oral Federal No. 6, Buenos Aires, case 1351 (Plan Sistemático), verdict 5 July 2012, as summarised by the International Crimes Database and MercoPress (6 July 2012)

cases.n: Argentina — Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo: 140 stolen grandchildren identified
cases.victims_note: about 500 children estimated kidnapped or born in detention centres; 140 identified by 7 July 2025; around 300 still unfound per Buenos Aires Times
cases.who: Argentine military regime (1976–83); military families and regime allies who received children
cases.cover: Children were illegally adopted with their original identities hidden; many did not know they were adopted.
cases.d: The Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo were founded in 1977 to find children kidnapped with their disappeared parents or born to mothers in detention, who were passed for adoption to military families and regime allies. Their work led to the creation of Argentina's National Bank of Genetic Data. On 7 July 2025 they announced the 140th grandchild identified: a man born on 17 April 1977 at the clandestine centre 'La Escuelita' in Bahía Blanca after his parents were kidnapped in Cutral Có, Neuquén. The Grandmothers had found 97 grandchildren by 2008 and 133 by July 2023.
cases.cite: Buenos Aires Times, 7 July 2025; AP, 28 July 2023 (133rd); Wikipedia 'Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo'

cases.n: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.victims_note: violations confirmed in at least 56 of 367 petitions; more than 140,000 (TRC) to about 200,000 (AP) Korean children sent abroad since the 1950s
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.cover: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.
cases.d: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cite: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Korea, findings announced 26 March 2025 (Reuters via The Star); Wikipedia 'International adoption of South Korean children'

cases.n: Spain — Dr Eduardo Vela, first 'stolen baby' trial: guilty but not punished
cases.who: Gynaecologist Eduardo Vela
cases.d: On 8 October 2018 a Madrid court found retired gynaecologist Eduardo Vela, 85, responsible for abducting a newborn, faking a birth and falsifying official documents (the forged birth certificate was dated 1969), but acquitted him because the statute of limitations had run, counting from when the child reached adulthood in 1987. It was the first trial in Spain over the 'stolen babies' of the Franco era and after. A judge had recorded about 30,000 cases of Spanish children taken, according to the report.
cases.cite: RTÉ News, 8 October 2018 (Madrid Provincial Court verdict)

cases.n: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–)
cases.victims_note: up to 20,000 estimated by investigators; the 2018 criminal probe covers about 8,000 overseas adoptions 1970–1999
cases.who: Chilean state agencies, hospital and social-service staff, intermediaries
cases.d: Children were taken from mainly poor mothers, some told their babies had died, and sent for adoption to families in the United States and Europe, including Sweden; the practice peaked under the Pinochet dictatorship (1973–1990). A Chilean judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad from 1970 to 1999. A congressional committee concluded the state was responsible; as of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice. Sweden opened its own investigation into intercountry adoptions after activism by Chilean adoptees.
cases.cite: Al Jazeera, 'How Chile's stolen children are finding their way home', 20 September 2023

cases.n: Ireland — Mother and Baby Homes Commission: 9,000 child deaths; adoptions abroad
cases.place: 18 institutions incl. Tuam (Co. Galway), Bessborough (Cork), Sean Ross Abbey (Roscrea)
cases.victims_note: about 56,000 women and 57,000 children passed through the investigated homes; about 9,000 children died
cases.who: Religious orders (incl. Bon Secours Sisters), local authorities and the Irish state
cases.cover: In May 2018 Tusla referred 126 cases of births falsely registered by the St Patrick's Guild adoption agency (illegal registrations that hid children's identities).
cases.d: The Commission of Investigation's final report (published 12 January 2021) covered 14 mother and baby homes and 4 county homes. About 9,000 children died in them between 1922 and 1998, about one in seven births and about twice the general infant mortality rate. Several homes had been linked to illegal domestic and foreign adoptions, many to the United States. On 13 January 2021 Taoiseach Micheál Martin apologised for a 'profound generational wrong'. (The care agent may hold the home-conditions record; this record focuses on removals and adoptions.)
cases.cite: Mother and Baby Homes Commission of Investigation, Final Report, 12 January 2021, as summarised by Wikipedia

cases.n: Australia — forced adoptions: Senate inquiry 2012 and national apology 2013
cases.victims_note: 'around 250,000 adoptions' is described as feasible; an unknown share involved forced removal from single mothers
cases.who: Australian governments, hospitals, churches and adoption agencies
cases.d: From the 1950s to the 1980s babies of unmarried mothers were taken for adoption, often without informed consent. The Senate Community Affairs References Committee reported on 29 February 2012 ('Commonwealth Contribution to Former Forced Adoption Policies and Practices'). Prime Minister Julia Gillard delivered a national apology on 21 March 2013, after state apologies starting with Western Australia (19 October 2010), South Australia, ACT, NSW and Victoria in 2012.
cases.cite: Senate Community Affairs References Committee report, 29 Feb 2012; National Apology for Forced Adoptions, 21 March 2013 (via Wikipedia 'Forced adoption in Australia')

cases.n: Australia — Stolen Generations: Bringing Them Home (1997) and national apology (2008)
cases.victims_note: between one in three and one in ten Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children removed in some regions (Bringing Them Home); Robert Manne estimated 20,000–25,000
cases.who: Australian federal, state and territory governments; church and state missions and institutions
cases.d: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children were forcibly removed from their families under government policies roughly between 1910 and 1970 and placed in institutions, missions, foster or adoptive families. The Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission's 1997 report 'Bringing Them Home' found that between one in three and one in ten children were separated in some regions. Prime Minister Kevin Rudd apologised on 13 February 2008. Redress schemes followed: Tasmania (2006, A$5m), NSW (2017, A$75,000 per survivor) and a A$378m Commonwealth scheme for NT, ACT and Jervis Bay (announced 6 August 2021).
cases.cite: HREOC, Bringing Them Home, 1997; Wikipedia 'Stolen Generations'

cases.n: Canada — Sixties Scoop: Ontario ruling 2017 and C$800m settlement
cases.victims_note: about 20,000 Indigenous children estimated
cases.who: Federal government of Canada and provincial child welfare authorities
cases.d: From the late 1950s into the 1980s about 20,000 Indigenous children were taken from their families and fostered or adopted, mostly into white middle-class families, some in the United States. On 14 February 2017 Justice Edward Belobaba of the Ontario Superior Court (Brown v. Canada, 2017 ONSC 251) found Canada breached its duty of care to prevent on-reserve children in Ontario from losing their Aboriginal identity. On 6 October 2017 an C$800 million settlement was announced, paying C$25,000–50,000 per eligible status First Nations or Inuit former ward, plus a C$50m healing foundation.
cases.cite: Brown v. Canada (Attorney General), 2017 ONSC 251; settlement announced 6 October 2017 (via Wikipedia 'Sixties Scoop')

cases.n: United States — Indian Adoption Project (1958–67) and the Indian Child Welfare Act 1978
cases.place: Washington, D.C. (Bureau of Indian Affairs) — placements in many states
cases.victims_note: 395 children placed under the official project; thousands more through other agencies in the same period
cases.who: Bureau of Indian Affairs, US Children's Bureau, Child Welfare League of America
cases.d: The Indian Adoption Project placed 395 Native American children with white families between 1958 and 1967. Congress passed the Indian Child Welfare Act in 1978 after hearings described the 'wholesale separation of Indian children from their families'. In June 2001 the Child Welfare League of America's executive director said the project was 'wrong' and 'hurtful'.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Indian Adoption Project' citing H.R. Rep. 95-1386 (1978) and CWLA statement, June 2001

cases.n: Israel — Yemenite, Mizrahi and Balkan children affair
cases.victims_note: claims range from 1,000 to 5,000 children; the 2001 Kedmi commission examined over 800 cases
cases.who: Israeli state health and immigration institutions
cases.d: Families, mostly Yemenite immigrants, said babies taken to hospitals in 1948–1954 disappeared and were told they had died. Three state inquiries (1967, 1988, 2001) concluded most had died; the 2001 Kedmi commission examined over 800 cases, finding 750 deaths and 56 unresolved, and the 1967 committee found 2 adoptions. About 400,000 documents were released on 28 December 2016. In February 2021 the government expressed sorrow and approved compensation of up to NIS 200,000 per family whose child's fate is unknown.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Yemenite Children Affair' (citing Haaretz, Times of Israel, BBC)

cases.n: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
cases.place: Occupied Poland (Łódź region, Zamość and others)
cases.victims_note: Polish official estimate about 200,000; other estimates 20,000–200,000; only 10–20% returned
cases.who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
cases.d: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn or health-department camps and placed them with German families under new identities. The RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., eighth of the 12 Nuremberg follow-up trials, 10 October 1947 – 10 March 1948) ruled that the abductions and Germanization were part of genocide. Heinemann's research identified 20,000 Polish children who passed Germanization criteria; about 1,000 were taken from Bohemia and Moravia and 1,100 from Slovenia.
cases.cite: Nuremberg Military Tribunal, RuSHA case, judgment 10 March 1948; Wikipedia 'Kidnapping of children by Nazi Germany'

cases.n: France — Children of Creuse: 2,015 Réunionese children moved to mainland France
cases.victims_note: 2,015 children per the page body (2,150 in its lead)
cases.who: French state social services (DDASS); scheme led by Réunion MP Michel Debré
cases.d: Between 1963 and 1982 the French state declared Réunionese children wards of the state, often after parents signed abandonment papers they could not read, and moved them to depopulating rural departments of mainland France. Some were adopted; others stayed in homes or worked unpaid on farms. The newspaper Témoignages denounced 'child trafficking' in August 1968. In 2014 the National Assembly passed a resolution recognising the state failed its 'moral responsibility' to the children.
cases.cite: French National Assembly resolution, 18 February 2014 (via Wikipedia 'Children of Creuse')

cases.n: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.victims_note: more than 11,000 babies adopted to Western countries in the 1980s (Zembla); about 4,000 to the Netherlands
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.cover: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.
cases.d: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
cases.cite: The Guardian, 20 September 2017 (Karen McVeigh); BBC News, 14 March 2021

cases.n: Vietnam — Nam Dinh ring: 266 babies sold for foreign adoption
cases.who: Heads of two provincial social welfare centres; doctors and nurses at village clinics
cases.d: In September 2009 a court in Nam Dinh tried 16 people, including the head of two social welfare centres and village clinic doctors and nurses, for 'abuse of power and authority'. They allegedly solicited infants from poor families and falsified documents saying the babies were abandoned; 266 babies were sent for foreign adoption from 2005 to July 2008. In April 2008 the US embassy in Hanoi had reported desertion numbers rising 17-fold or more at orphanages in 7 provinces, and Vietnam did not renew its adoption agreement with the US when it expired in September 2008.
cases.cite: The Independent, 23 September 2009; Schuster Institute (Brandeis), 'Vietnam' adoption timeline

cases.n: China — Hunan orphanages bought trafficked babies for adoption (2005 convictions)
cases.place: Hengyang, Hunan (six orphanages); babies brought from Guangdong
cases.victims_note: nearly 1,000 children bought by six orphanages in three years (court documents reviewed by ABC News)
cases.who: Six state orphanages in Hunan; traffickers from Guangdong; local officials
cases.d: Six Hunan orphanages were found buying infants from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong, placing nearly 1,000 children with domestic and foreign families between 2002 and 2005. In 2005, according to Xinhua, 23 civil officials were fired; three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years and six others to 3–13 years.
cases.cite: Schuster Institute for Investigative Journalism (Brandeis), 'China' adoption page, citing Xinhua and ABC News

cases.n: Cambodia — Lauryn Galindo adoption-fraud conspiracy; US moratorium 2001
cases.victims_note: about 800 adoptions facilitated 1997–2001; guilty plea covered 17 cases
cases.who: US facilitator Lauryn Galindo and associates; Cambodian officials paid by facilitators
cases.d: The US imposed a moratorium on Cambodian adoptions in late 2001 after fraudulent cases and raids by the Cambodian rights group LICADHO. Facilitator Lauryn Galindo arranged about 800 adoptions for US families in 1997–2001, more than half of all Cambodian adoptions; the US government said her business paid Cambodian mothers for babies. In 2004 she pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit visa fraud and money laundering in 17 cases, admitting she falsified documents that erased children's identities (she denied trafficking), and faced an 18-month sentence. Some adoptive families later found their children had living relatives.
cases.cite: ABC News 20/20, 24 March 2005; Schuster Institute (Brandeis) Cambodia page

cases.n: Samoa — Focus on Children (Utah) adoption fraud
cases.victims_note: 80 adoptions 2002–2005; 37 questioned in the indictment
cases.who: Focus on Children, Utah agency run by Scott and Karen Banks
cases.d: Samoan parents were told their children would go to the US temporarily for schooling, but the children were adopted permanently. A federal indictment on 28 February 2007 charged Scott and Karen Banks and three others with alien smuggling, visa fraud and money laundering. All pleaded guilty on 6 January 2009 to misdemeanour counts of aiding the improper entry of an alien, and the agency to a felony conspiracy; in February 2009 Judge David Sam sentenced them to five years' probation and banned them from adoption work.
cases.cite: Schuster Institute (Brandeis), 'Samoa' adoption page, citing ICE press release 1 March 2007

cases.n: Marshall Islands — Paul Petersen 'baby mill' adoption scheme
cases.victims_note: Utah investigators believed more than 40 pregnant women were brought through Utah
cases.who: Paul Petersen, Maricopa County (Arizona) Assessor and adoption lawyer
cases.d: Petersen, an elected Arizona official, paid recruiters to bring pregnant Marshallese women to the US, paying them about $10,000 to give up their babies and charging adoptive couples about $35,000, although the Compact of Free Association bars Marshallese travel to the US for adoption. Charged in October 2019 in Utah, Arizona and Arkansas, he pleaded guilty in all three courts in June 2020 (human smuggling, fraud, communication fraud) and was sentenced in December 2020 in federal court in Arkansas to more than six years in prison. He also fraudulently obtained about $814,000 in Arizona Medicaid funds for the women.
cases.cite: Utah Attorney General press release, 19 June 2020; USA Today, 1 December 2020 (via Wikipedia 'Paul Petersen (criminal)')

cases.n: Uganda — European Adoption Consultants bribery scheme; judges sanctioned
cases.victims_note: more than 30 Ugandan children
cases.who: European Adoption Consultants (Ohio, defunct); Ugandan lawyers and judges
cases.cover: Bribes were paid to Ugandan judges and other officials to secure adoption orders.
cases.d: Between 2013 and 2016 the Ohio agency European Adoption Consultants arranged the adoption of more than 30 Ugandan children by US families; families were promised their children would attend school in Kampala but they were taken to an unlicensed home. On 14 August 2020 a federal indictment charged two EAC employees and Ugandan lawyer Dorah Mirembe (allegations; presumed innocent); an earlier employee, Robin Longoria, pleaded guilty in August 2019 to bribing Ugandan officials. On 17–18 August 2020 the US State Department sanctioned Ugandan judges Moses Mukiibi and Wilson Musalu Musene and lawyers Mirembe and Patrick Ecobu.
cases.cite: US Department of Justice press release, 17 August 2020; The Guardian, 18 August 2020

cases.n: Guatemala — notary-run adoption trade to the US (1996–2007)
cases.victims_note: 5,577 adopted abroad in 2007 alone, 4,728 to the US; up to 500 kidnapping cases believed linked to children adopted overseas; a 2003 government commission documented 1,084 missing children incl. 500 under one presumed abducted for adoption
cases.who: Private notaries (notarios), baby brokers, foster homes, officials
cases.d: After the civil war ended in 1996, adoptions abroad rose each year, run almost entirely (about 98%) by private notaries who handled both sides without court review and charged $35,000 or more per child; 97% of children went to the US. CICIG's 2010 report studied 153 cases and found 78% violated the new law in some way. Guatemala passed a Hague-compliant law on 11 December 2007 and stopped new adoptions to the US from 1 January 2008; the US State Department announced on 9 January 2008 it would not allow new adoptions until procedures were compliant.
cases.cite: CICIG, Report on Players Involved in the Illegal Adoption Process in Guatemala, 2010 (via Wikipedia); Schuster Institute (Brandeis) 'Guatemala'

cases.n: Guatemala — Casa Quivira raid: 46 children possibly stolen for adoption
cases.who: Casa Quivira private adoption home (run by a US citizen and his Guatemalan wife); two lawyers
cases.d: On 11 August 2007 Guatemalan police found 46 children aged a few days to three years at the Casa Quivira adoption home in Antigua after neighbours reported foreigners collecting children daily. Two lawyers who allegedly processed the adoptions were arrested. Attorney General Mario Gordillo said most of the children lacked proper documents and his office was investigating whether they had been stolen or obtained from mothers under coercion.
cases.cite: The Guardian (staff and agencies), 13 August 2007

cases.n: India — Andhra Pradesh adoption racket (Tender Loving Care Home)
cases.who: St Teresa's Tender Loving Care Home and other agencies
cases.d: On 22 March 2001 Hyderabad police arrested a man carrying three baby girls allegedly bound for St Teresa's Tender Loving Care Home; other agencies were also flagged. A chargesheet said the home earned Rs 3.33 crore from intercountry adoptions, mainly to the US, in 1999–2001. On 31 August 2005 Sister Teresa Maria Kattikaran and nine others were sentenced to six months' imprisonment for cheating and forgery, and Andhra Pradesh became the first state to bar private agencies from placing children.
cases.cite: Schuster Institute (Brandeis), 'India', citing Frontline (28 April 2001, 2005) and The Hindu (26 Dec 2002, 31 Aug 2005)

cases.n: India — Malaysian Social Services, Chennai: children kidnapped for adoption
cases.victims_note: police suspected more than 350 children; files for 120 sent overseas, at least 13 to Australia
cases.who: Malaysian Social Services adoption agency
cases.d: Police suspected the family running the Malaysian Social Services agency since 1991 of kidnapping and trafficking more than 350 children; in May 2005 Chennai police arrested three family members and six others. Children allegedly had their appearance changed and histories fabricated; officers found files for 120 children sent overseas. TIME reported in 2008 that Australian authorities had earlier warnings.
cases.cite: Schuster Institute (Brandeis), 'India', citing Boloji (12 June 2005) and TIME (21 August 2008)

cases.n: India — Preet Mandir, Pune: CBI case on inter-country adoption racket
cases.victims_note: agency placed 518 children 2004–2006, most internationally
cases.who: Preet Mandir adoption agency; state officials
cases.d: Preet Mandir placed 518 children in 2004–2006, most abroad, and Frontline reported in 2005 it handled about 7% of India's foreign adoptions while charging high 'donation' fees. CNN-IBN reported in December 2007 that the CBI had confirmed findings on illegal adoptions. On 18 May 2010 the CBI registered a case against a managing trustee and state officials over an alleged inter-country adoption racket.
cases.cite: Schuster Institute (Brandeis), 'India'

cases.n: Nepal — baby-buying in intercountry adoption; 2007 shutdown
cases.victims_note: 394 intercountry adoptions in 2006, up from 8 in 2000
cases.who: Orphanages and adoption intermediaries
cases.d: A Daily Telegraph investigation in March 2007 described baby-buying, bribes and deception of birth families. In April 2007 Nepal's new minister halted all intercountry adoptions, leaving about 400 Western families waiting; about 440 pending cases were processed after November 2007, and new rules were published in May 2008. UNICEF and Terre des hommes published 'Adopting: The Rights of the Child' in August 2008. Wikipedia records that the US later suspended adoptions of children declared abandoned because documents were unreliable.
cases.cite: Schuster Institute (Brandeis), 'Nepal'; Wikipedia 'International adoption'

cases.n: United States — Georgia Tann / Tennessee Children's Home Society black-market adoptions
cases.victims_note: about 5,000 children estimated stolen; 3,000 placed in New York and California alone 1940–1950
cases.who: Tennessee Children's Home Society (Shelby County branch) under Georgia Tann
cases.d: From 1924 to 1950 Georgia Tann used the Memphis branch of the Tennessee Children's Home Society to take children from poor families and sell them, charging up to $5,000 for out-of-state adoptions when Tennessee adoptions cost about $7. A state investigation into adoption fraud led to the home's closure in 1950; Tann died before its findings were published.
cases.cite: Tennessee State Library and Archives, Georgia Tann/Tennessee Children's Home Society Investigation Scrapbooks, 1950 (via Wikipedia 'Georgia Tann')

cases.n: South Korea — Brothers Home children sent overseas for adoption
cases.victims_note: at least 31 children improperly sent overseas (TRC, Feb 2025); AP found evidence of 19 adoptions 1979–1986
cases.who: Brothers Home (Busan detention facility); receiving agencies named by AP incl. Holt International, Children's Home Society of Minnesota
cases.d: Brothers Home was a state-backed facility where people deemed vagrants were confined and forced to work; the TRC recognised state culpability on 23 August 2022 and counted 657 deaths there 1975–1988. An AP investigation (November 2019) found Brothers Home organised the adoption of 19 children abroad in 1979–1986 and that six US agencies received children from it. In February 2025 the TRC confirmed at least 31 children were improperly sent overseas for adoption through the facility.
cases.cite: AP, 9 November 2019; Korea Times, 22 February 2025 (TRC finding)

cases.n: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.cover: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).
cases.d: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cite: Commissie Onderzoek Interlandelijke Adoptie (Joustra), report 8 February 2021, as reported by BBC News, 14 March 2021; Dutch Wikipedia 'Interlandelijke adoptie'

cases.n: United Kingdom — forced adoption of unmarried mothers' babies 1949–1976 (JCHR 2022; apology 2026)
cases.victims_note: about 185,000 babies of unmarried mothers adopted in England and Wales 1949–1976 (JCHR estimate)
cases.who: Local authorities, religious organisations, NHS bodies, mother and baby homes
cases.d: The Joint Committee on Human Rights report 'The Violation of Family Life: Adoption of Children of Unmarried Women 1949–1976' (15 July 2022) found many mothers did not want to give up their babies and were pressured by secrecy, shame and lack of support, and rejected the government's position that it was not responsible. The government declined to apologise in March 2023. On 2 July 2026 Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer gave a formal apology in the House of Commons, calling the practices 'embedded' across local authorities, religious organisations and parts of what is now the NHS, and announced a £4m support package (no compensation scheme).
cases.cite: Joint Committee on Human Rights, HC 270, 15 July 2022; BBC News, 2 July 2026

cases.n: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban
cases.victims_note: DCI listed over 4,000 children to 22 countries Aug 1990–Feb 1991; figures as high as 10,000 for March 1990–June 1991 (Selman 2002)
cases.who: Private adoption agencies and intermediaries; Romanian authorities
cases.d: After Ceaușescu's fall, television images of about 100,000 children in orphanages led to an adoption boom; private agencies charged €7,500–25,000 and the system 'quickly became awash in corruption' (DW). Romania halted adoptions in June 1991 and, under EU pressure, passed a law in June 2004 banning all foreign adoptions except by grandparents. The European Parliament's rapporteur Baroness Emma Nicholson had criticised 'international adoption and child trafficking' in Romania. Romania's own HCCH return shows 458 intercountry adoptions in 2002, 332 in 2003, 2 in 2005 and 0 in 2006.
cases.cite: Deutsche Welle, 22 June 2004; Selman, Population Research and Policy Review 21 (2002); Romania annual statistics to HCCH

cases.n: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.victims_note: more than 15,000 Ethiopian children adopted in the US since 1999 (BBC)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.d: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.
cases.cite: BBC News, 10 January 2018; Schuster Institute (Brandeis) 'Ethiopia'

cases.n: Russia — Dima Yakovlev Law bans adoption by US citizens
cases.victims_note: over 1,000 adoptions in progress at the time, including about 200 children already told they would be adopted
cases.who: Russian state
cases.d: Federal Law 272-FZ, signed by President Putin on 28 December 2012 and effective 1 January 2013, banned US citizens from adopting Russian children. It was named after Dima Yakovlev, a Russian toddler who died in July 2008 after his adoptive father left him in a car in Virginia, and was widely seen as retaliation for the US Magnitsky Act. In April 2010 a US adoptive mother had sent her 7-year-old adopted son alone on a flight back to Moscow, prompting Russian calls for a suspension. (This is a closure event, not a trafficking finding.)
cases.cite: Kremlin.ru, 28 December 2012; Federal Law 272-FZ (via Wikipedia 'Dima Yakovlev Law')

cases.n: Haiti — New Life Children's Refuge: US missionaries try to take 33 children after earthquake
cases.place: Calebasse and Le Citron, near Port-au-Prince → Dominican border
cases.who: New Life Children's Refuge (Idaho Baptist missionaries) led by Laura Silsby
cases.d: On 29 January 2010, after the earthquake, ten American Baptist missionaries were arrested trying to take 33 children across the Dominican border without authorisation; SOS Children's Villages reported most, if not all, were not orphans. They were charged on 4 February 2010 with kidnapping and criminal association; nine were released. On 17 May 2010 leader Laura Silsby was convicted of arranging irregular travel and sentenced to time served.
cases.cite: CNN, 5 February 2010; BBC, 5 February 2010 (via Wikipedia 'New Life Children's Refuge case')

cases.n: Vietnam — Operation Babylift (1975): not all children were orphans
cases.victims_note: over 3,300 airlifted (figures vary); over 2,500 adopted abroad, about 250 to Australia
cases.who: US government (Military Airlift Command); Holt International, Friends of Children of Viet Nam, Friends For All Children and other agencies
cases.d: In April 1975 the US airlifted over 3,300 infants and children out of South Vietnam; the first flight, on 4 April, crashed killing 78 children. A lawsuit filed on 29 April 1975 on behalf of the Committee to Protect the Rights of Vietnamese Children alleged that many children were not orphans and were taken without parents' consent; many had been placed in orphanages by living relatives.
cases.cite: New York Times, 1 May 1975; USAID Operation Babylift Report 1975 (via Wikipedia 'Operation Babylift')

cases.n: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda)
cases.victims_note: close to 1,000 documented cases of disappeared children
cases.who: Salvadoran armed forces
cases.cover: The armed forces have not granted access to archives on disappeared children despite years of lobbying.
cases.d: Pro-Búsqueda, founded in 1994, has documented close to a thousand children disappeared during the Salvadoran civil war, mostly by the armed forces; many were adopted through flawed procedures to the US, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands. On 1 March 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the 1982 disappearance of the Serrano Cruz sisters during the 'Guinda de Mayo' military operation. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010.
cases.cite: Inter-American Court of Human Rights, Serrano-Cruz Sisters v. El Salvador, 1 March 2005; Wikipedia 'Pro-Búsqueda'

cases.n: China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases
cases.victims_note: about 160,000 children sent abroad since 1992, more than half to the US (New Yorker)
cases.who: China Center for Children's Welfare and Adoption; state orphanages
cases.d: China opened intercountry adoption in 1992; about 160,000 children were sent abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the US in 2005. The programme came to depend increasingly on abuse, abduction and trafficking (New Yorker), including Hunan orphanages buying trafficked babies (2005). On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry announced the end of the programme, except adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.
cases.cite: The New Yorker (Barbara Demick), 19 September 2024; FOX 6, 5 September 2024

cases.n: Spain — children of Republican prisoners taken by the Franco regime
cases.place: Women's prisons and Auxilio Social homes across Spain
cases.victims_note: 30,960 children removed from Republican mothers 1944–1954; Garzón: more than 30,000 under state 'tutelage'
cases.who: Franco regime; Auxilio Social; Women's Protection Board (Patronato de Protección a la Mujer); Falange
cases.cover: Names were changed so children could be given to pro-regime families; the 1977 Amnesty Law has hindered investigation, and many Women's Protection Board files went missing in 1996.
cases.d: A 1940 law allowed imprisoned mothers to keep children only until age three, after which the state took custody; 12,043 Republican children were in state custody in 1943. In 2008 Judge Baltasar Garzón characterised the removals as crimes against humanity and said the Falange was involved in kidnapping or forcibly repatriating children and changing their names. In January 2011 families of 261 babies who disappeared from hospitals over about fifty years took their cases to the attorney general; lawyers' estimates of up to 300,000 were rejected by a 2026 forensic study, which did not dispute about 30,000 children placed in state care.
cases.cite: Audiencia Nacional, Garzón ruling (El País, 2008); Wikipedia 'Lost children of Francoism'

cases.n: Kenya — babies stolen and sold in Nairobi, incl. from a government hospital (BBC Africa Eye)
cases.place: Nairobi (Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital; Kayole street clinics)
cases.victims_note: Missing Child Kenya worked on about 600 missing-child cases in four years; no official statistics exist
cases.who: Street child-snatchers working for a buyer; illegal street clinics; a clinical social worker at a government hospital
cases.d: A year-long BBC Africa Eye investigation (November 2020) found children snatched from homeless mothers in Nairobi and sold for about £350–550, illegal street clinics selling newborns (one offered an unborn child for about £315 while paying the mother £70), and a clinical social worker at the government-run Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital who sold an abandoned two-week-old boy to undercover reporters for 300,000 shillings (£2,000) using legitimate transfer paperwork. The reporters delivered all the children to a children's home. The BBC said the official appeared to keep his job and the clinic appeared to still operate.
cases.cite: BBC Africa Eye, 'The baby stealers', 15 November 2020

cases.n: Nigeria — Aba 'baby farm': 32 pregnant girls freed
cases.who: Cross Foundation clinic proprietor
cases.d: In late May 2011 Abia State police raided the Cross Foundation clinic in Aba and rescued 32 pregnant girls, mostly aged 15–17, allegedly held so their babies could be sold for illegal adoption or ritual use; four babies already sold were recovered. The proprietor was arrested, according to police commissioner Bala Hassan. Nigerian police had uncovered a network of 'baby farms' posing as orphanages in Enugu in 2008, and more were found in later years (five in 2013, eight in 2015 per Makinde et al.).
cases.cite: The Guardian, 2 June 2011; Makinde et al., Trauma, Violence & Abuse (2015)

cases.n: Nigeria — Lagos raid: 162 children rescued from 'baby factory' and unregistered orphanages
cases.d: In April 2018 Lagos State Commissioner for Youths and Social Development Agboola Dabiri said 100 girls and 62 boys had been rescued from a 'baby factory' and two unregistered orphanages; some had been sexually abused. The BBC noted babies from such places can be sold for adoption, child labour or trafficking, and that in 2013 17 pregnant teenagers and 11 babies were rescued from a house in Imo State.
cases.cite: BBC News (AFP), 26 April 2018

cases.n: Indonesia — baby trafficking syndicate selling infants to Singapore
cases.place: Pontianak (West Kalimantan) and Tangerang; babies from West Java
cases.victims_note: at least 25 babies sold since 2023; six rescued
cases.who: Syndicate of recruiters, caretakers and document forgers
cases.d: In July 2025 West Java police said a syndicate had sold at least 25 babies since 2023, mostly to buyers in Singapore, some 'reserved while still in the womb', for 11–16 million rupiah each, after preparing fraudulent family cards and passports in Pontianak. Thirteen people were arrested and six babies about to be trafficked were rescued; police sought Interpol help to trace the adopters.
cases.cite: BBC News, 17 July 2025

cases.n: Thailand — 'Baby 101' surrogate baby-breeding operation
cases.who: Baby 101 company
cases.d: In February 2011 Thai police freed 14 Vietnamese women, half of them pregnant, held in two Bangkok houses with passports confiscated by a company called Baby 101 that took orders from childless couples for newborns. A Taiwanese woman said to run the operation was charged with human trafficking; four said they had been tricked, and the health minister said some appeared to have been raped.
cases.cite: HuffPost (AFP), 24 February 2011

cases.n: Chad — Zoé's Ark tries to fly 103 children to France (convicted 2007)
cases.who: French charity L'Arche de Zoé (founder Éric Breteau)
cases.d: On 30 October 2007 six members of the French charity Zoé's Ark were charged in Chad with abducting 103 children they said were Darfur orphans to be fostered in France; most were found to be Chadian with at least one living parent or guardian. The six were convicted on 26 December 2007 and sentenced to eight years' forced labour (to be served in France) and ordered to pay restitution to each of the 103 children; a Chadian and a Sudanese national got four years, and two Chadian officials were acquitted. Chad's president pardoned the six in March 2008.
cases.cite: BBC News, 29 October 2007; Wikipedia 'Zoé's Ark'

cases.n: Canada — Ideal Maternity Home ('Butterbox Babies'), Nova Scotia
cases.victims_note: 800–1,500 babies born there 1928–1946
cases.who: William Peach Young and Lila Gladys Young
cases.d: The unlicensed Ideal Maternity Home charged unmarried mothers $500 and sold babies on the black market for up to $10,000, including across borders. The Nova Scotia Department of Public Welfare gathered evidence from 1934; the Youngs were convicted of fraud in 1935, acquitted of manslaughter in 1936, and convicted in 1946 on seven violations of the Maternity Boarding Houses Act before the home was shut. A 1946 Montreal Standard article called them international traffickers in babies.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Ideal Maternity Home' (citing Bette Cahill, Butterbox Babies, 1992)

cases.n: Denmark — 1951 'little Danes' experiment: 22 Greenlandic children removed
cases.who: Danish government, Danish Red Cross, Save the Children Denmark
cases.d: In May 1951 Danish authorities, with the Red Cross and Save the Children, sent 22 Greenlandic Inuit children to Danish foster families to re-educate them as 'little Danes'; they were supposed to be orphans but only six were. Six were adopted in Denmark and 16 returned to a Danish-speaking orphanage in Greenland and never lived with their families again. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised in December 2020, and in March 2022 the six survivors were awarded 250,000 kroner each.
cases.cite: BBC News, 9 March 2022; KNR, 28 February 2022 (via Wikipedia 'Little Danes experiment')

cases.n: Ukraine — Ukrainian children given Russian citizenship and adopted into Russian families
cases.victims_note: almost 20,000 children transferred (Ukrainian figure); adoption-specific numbers not established
cases.who: Russian state; Children's Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova
cases.d: On 30 May 2022 President Putin signed a decree easing Russian citizenship for Ukrainian children so they could be adopted by Russian families; Russia created a register of families wishing to adopt Ukrainian children and paid families per adopted child granted citizenship. Lvova-Belova said she had adopted a child from Mariupol herself. On 17 March 2023 the ICC issued arrest warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova for unlawful deportation and transfer of children. Yale HRL (14 February 2023) documented a 'systematic' programme of re-education and adoption. (Deportations and camps are recorded by the conflict agent; this record covers the adoption element.)
cases.cite: ICC arrest warrants, 17 March 2023; Yale School of Public Health HRL, 'Russia's Systematic Program for the Re-education & Adoption of Ukraine's Children', 14 February 2023

cases.n: France — state report finds 'illicit practices of a systemic nature' in intercountry adoption
cases.who: French government and adoption associations
cases.cover: The report said public authorities were alerted early, including at the highest levels, and were late in taking action.
cases.d: In March 2024 France released an assessment acknowledging that its government had long known of 'the existence of illicit practices of a systemic nature' in intercountry adoption, and that diplomatic and association archives showed these practices existed in countries over long periods. France received 11,165 Korean children 1968–2008 among others.
cases.cite: French inter-ministerial inspection report on illicit practices in intercountry adoption, March 2024, as quoted by AP/PBS Frontline, 20 September 2024

cases.n: Norway — state investigation of illegal intercountry adoptions (2023–)
cases.who: Norwegian state; private adoption organisations
cases.d: Norway launched an investigation in 2023 into whether illegal or unethical practices occurred in intercountry adoptions and whether Norwegian officials failed to control them; the foreign ministry said it was 'aware of serious findings' (AP, 2024). Norway received 6,295 Korean children 1955–2008, and in 1974–75 Scandinavian diplomats pressed South Korea to keep sending children after it tried to stop. In September 2025 a Korean-born adoptee served notice of a lawsuit against the Norwegian state alleging her adoption was illegal (allegation).
cases.cite: AP/PBS Frontline, 20 September 2024; The Oslo Desk, 23 September 2025

cases.n: Greece — about 4,000 children adopted abroad 1950–1975; 2025 citizenship law
cases.victims_note: as many as 4,000 Greek-born children
cases.who: Greek state institutions and foundling homes; AHEPA and other US agencies and proxy-adoption intermediaries
cases.cover: The adoptions were covered by confidentiality and secrecy; many adoptees lacked papers proving their origins.
cases.d: Between 1950 and 1975 as many as 4,000 Greek-born children, many called 'orphans' after the civil war or born 'illegitimate', were adopted in the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden through hastily conducted procedures. A law published on 2 May 2025 recognised their adopted status, restored a path to Greek citizenship and eased access to records. The Greek state promised an investigation in the late 1950s that has not been carried out.
cases.cite: Gonda Van Steen, History & Policy policy paper (2025); Van Steen, Adoption, Memory, and Cold War Greece (University of Michigan Press, 2019)

cases.n: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.d: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.
cases.cite: Van Steen, History & Policy (2025), on the Swedish report of 2 June 2025; AP/PBS Frontline, 20 September 2024

cases.n: Switzerland — authorities' irregularities in intercountry adoptions (Sri Lanka, India, Tibet…); proposed ban
cases.who: Swiss federal and cantonal authorities; private adoption agencies
cases.d: Swiss authorities knew that children placed for adoption, often wrongly presented as orphans, were linked to economic interests and organised child trafficking, yet decisions were made on incomplete or falsified documents and parental consent was not checked. After a 2018 parliamentary mandate for a study, the Federal Council acknowledged the authorities' irregularities and omissions in 2020 and 2023, and in late 2024 advocated a general ban on intercountry adoption. AP reported Switzerland 'apologized for failing to prevent illegal adoptions'.
cases.cite: Historical Dictionary of Switzerland, 'Adoption' (Urs Germann, 2025) via Wikipedia 'Adoption in Switzerland'; AP/PBS Frontline, 20 September 2024

cases.n: Switzerland — 'Kinder der Landstrasse': Yenish children removed by Pro Juventute (1926–1973)
cases.who: Pro Juventute foundation, with federal and cantonal authorities
cases.d: From 1926 to 1973 the Pro Juventute 'Hilfswerk für die Kinder der Landstrasse', backed by federal authorities, removed about 590 Yenish children from their families and placed them in foster homes, orphanages, psychiatric hospitals and prisons, with contact with parents systematically prevented. It ended after the Beobachter exposé of 15 April 1972. Victims later received a total of 11 million francs. In February 2025 the Swiss government acknowledged the persecution as a crime against humanity, following a September 2024 legal opinion. (Care agent covers Verdingkinder.)
cases.cite: Swiss Federal Archives study (1998); Federal Council summary of the Diggelmann/Emery/Rüfli opinion, 2025

cases.n: Sierra Leone — 29 Makeni children sent to US adopters without parents' consent (HANCI)
cases.who: Help A Needy Child International (HANCI)
cases.d: In 1998 about 29 children at HANCI's centre in Makeni were taken to Freetown for medical checks and never returned; parents later learned they had been adopted by Americans. Sierra Leone suspended adoptions on 21 May 2009. In April 2012 a presidential commission shut HANCI down and concluded the biological families 'cannot be said to have genuinely consented'.
cases.cite: Schuster Institute (Brandeis), 'Sierra Leone', citing AP (3 June 2010) and Slate (E.J. Graff, 11 May 2012)

cases.n: Liberia — post-war orphanage boom and adoption fraud
cases.victims_note: Hannah B. Williams Orphanage: 89 of 102 'orphans' returned to families in 2005; US orphan visas rose from 183 (2005) to 353 (2006)
cases.who: Private orphanages and adoption facilitators
cases.d: After the civil war ended in 2003 the number of private orphanages rose from 40 to 120. In 2005 the Hannah B. Williams Orphanage in Monrovia was closed and 89 of its 102 'orphans' returned to their families. A 2007 UNICEF/Holt International report found many children entered the adoption pipeline through fraud, including false promises to birth parents, and the UN Mission found unaccredited for-profit orphanages. Canada placed a moratorium on Liberian adoptions.
cases.cite: Schuster Institute (Brandeis), 'Liberia', citing BBC (13 Nov 2008), UNICEF/Holt (2007), UNMIL (2007)

cases.n: Uruguay — Gelman v. Uruguay: baby taken from disappeared mother (Operation Condor)
cases.who: Uruguayan Defense Information Service (SID); joint Argentine–Uruguayan commando under Operation Condor
cases.cover: Uruguay's 1986 Expiry Law was used to close the investigation in 2003.
cases.d: A pregnant 19-year-old Argentine detained in Buenos Aires in August 1976 was moved secretly to Montevideo, gave birth in a military hospital, and her baby was taken in December 1976 and left with a police officer's family, who raised her under another identity for 23 years. On 24 February 2011 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights found Uruguay responsible for enforced disappearance and suppression of the child's identity, and ruled the 1986 Expiry Law amnesty legally ineffective.
cases.cite: Inter-American Court of Human Rights, Gelman v. Uruguay, judgment 24 February 2011 (Series C No. 221)

cases.n: Colombia — 1981 ring selling Andean children abroad with forged papers
cases.victims_note: 'hundreds of poor Andean children'
cases.who: Adoption trafficking ring
cases.d: In 1981 the New York Times (Warren Hoge) reported that Colombian authorities had uncovered a multimillion-dollar ring in which hundreds of poor Andean children were taken or bought from their mothers and sold abroad with forged papers. In 2003 Interpol issued a detention order for the manager of an uncertified Costa Rica-based adoption agency suspected of trafficking babies from Colombia in 2000–2002 (suspect, not convicted).
cases.cite: New York Times, 1981, via Schuster Institute (Brandeis) 'Colombia'

cases.n: Haiti — 2007: children trafficked for international adoption returned to parents
cases.victims_note: 47 children returned (IOM); a later report cited 50 returned and 100 awaiting rescue
cases.who: A Haitian centre holding children awaiting international adoption
cases.d: In 2007 a Haitian centre was forced to return 47 children awaiting international adoption to their families, after misleading parents with payments and holding the children in 'inhumane conditions' for months or years, according to the International Organization for Migration. An October 2007 report said officials had returned 50 trafficked children with 100 more awaiting rescue.
cases.cite: IOM press briefing notes, 'Trafficked Children Returned Home', 2007; Schuster Institute (Brandeis) 'Haiti'

cases.n: United States — 'Baby Scoop Era' adoptions of unmarried mothers' babies (1945–1973)
cases.victims_note: up to 4 million parents had children placed for adoption 1945–1973; non-relative adoptions peaked at about 89,200 in 1970
cases.who: Maternity homes, adoption agencies, social workers
cases.d: From 1945 to 1973 up to 4 million US parents, mostly unmarried mothers, had children placed for adoption, often presented as the only option with little effort to help mothers keep their babies. Non-relative adoptions rose from about 33,800 in 1951 to 89,200 in 1970. No national official inquiry has been held (unlike Australia, Ireland and the UK).
cases.cite: The Adoption History Project (University of Oregon), 'Adoption Statistics'; Wikipedia 'Baby Scoop Era'

cases.n: Canada — maternity homes and post-war adoptions of unmarried mothers' babies
cases.victims_note: Wikipedia, citing the Anglican Journal, gives over 400,000 unmarried pregnant women targeted 1945–1988
cases.who: Maternity homes run mostly by the Catholic Church and the Salvation Army, some Anglican and United Church; Children's Aid Societies
cases.d: Women sent to maternity homes for unwed mothers after the Second World War say they were coerced into giving up babies they wanted to keep through shaming, intimidation and withholding information about alternatives such as social assistance; one woman later found her file recorded that she had wanted to take her baby home. Origins Canada asked the churches to support a parliamentary or Senate inquiry (Anglican Journal, May 2014).
cases.cite: Anglican Journal, 'Taken', 13 May 2014

cases.n: Malaysia — online baby-selling trade (Al Jazeera 101 East)
cases.who: Online brokers; baby sellers
cases.d: An undercover Al Jazeera 101 East investigation (24 November 2016) documented an online trade in which babies were advertised with photos and sold for thousands of dollars, with buyers choosing by gender, race and skin colour. Some babies went to couples wanting a child; others, it reported, were sold to traffickers. Immigrant sex workers who cannot legally bear children in Malaysia were among those giving up babies.
cases.cite: Al Jazeera 101 East, 'Malaysia: Babies for Sale', 24 November 2016

cases.n: United States / UK — 'internet twins' sold twice through an online adoption broker
cases.place: St Louis, Missouri; broker in El Cajon, California; twins taken to Wales
cases.who: Internet agency A Caring Heart (broker in California)
cases.d: In 2000–01 twin baby girls were placed through the online agency A Caring Heart first with a California couple and then with a couple from Wales who paid about £8,200; police in Wales took the twins into care in January 2001 and on 9 April 2001 the High Court ordered them returned to the US. The FBI raided the agency in March 2001; the broker was charged with wire fraud in 2003 but charges were dropped in 2005 for insufficient evidence. The case led to UK adoption reform.
cases.cite: The Guardian, 'The internet twins: timeline', 9 April 2001; CBS News, 14 March 2001 (via Wikipedia)

nets.n: Argentine military junta — systematic appropriation of children (with Operation Condor partners)
nets.reach_note: Uruguay: Gelman case (IACHR 2011), in which the child of an Argentine detainee was taken in Montevideo under Operation Condor. reach_est lists Condor partner states. They are listed because Condor ran there, not because a child-appropriation finding there was opened in this research. Paraguay: a military doctor accused in the Silvia Quintela case fled there in 1986.
nets.d: Federal Oral Tribunal No. 6 found in July 2012 that the junta ran a systematic plan to take children born to detained or disappeared mothers and give them to military families and regime allies; Videla received 50 years and Bignone 15. About 500 children are estimated to have been taken; 140 had been identified by July 2025.
nets.cite: Tribunal Oral Federal No. 6, 5 July 2012; Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo

nets.n: Franco regime child removals and Spain's 'stolen babies'
nets.d: The Franco regime, Auxilio Social and the Women's Protection Board removed about 30,000 children of Republican prisoners and took babies of confined women into the early 1980s; later hospital 'stolen baby' cases reached the courts from 2011, with the first trial (Dr Eduardo Vela, 2018) ending in acquittal on limitation grounds.
nets.cite: Wikipedia 'Lost children of Francoism'; RTÉ, 8 October 2018

nets.n: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA) and Lebensborn e.V.
nets.reach_note: Norway: Lebensborn homes are documented in the Lebensborn article but adoption-of-kidnapped-children findings here cover Poland, Bohemia-Moravia, Slovenia, Yugoslavia, Belarus, USSR.
nets.d: RuSHA racially screened children in occupied territories and Lebensborn ran camps and homes from which selected children were placed with German families under new identities. The Nuremberg RuSHA trial (1947–48) ruled the kidnapping and Germanization of children part of genocide.
nets.cite: Nuremberg Military Tribunal, US v. Greifelt et al. (RuSHA case)

nets.n: South Korea's four authorised overseas adoption agencies (Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
nets.reach_note: Receiving countries from the Korean Ministry of Health and Welfare table of adoptees by country 1953–2008; the TRC petitions came from 11 receiving countries.
nets.d: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). The TRC (March 2025) found agencies met monthly quotas for foreign partners, falsified orphan status and swapped identities, and that the state failed to supervise them. All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).
nets.cite: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Korea, 26 March 2025; AP/PBS Frontline, 20 September 2024; The Guardian, 28 September 2023

nets.d: Agency run by Scott and Karen Banks that arranged about 80 adoptions of Samoan children whose parents were told it was temporary schooling; the defendants pleaded guilty in January 2009 and were banned from adoption work.

Defunct Ohio agency that, per a 2020 federal indictment, procured more than 30 Ugandan children for US clients in 2013–2016 through bribery of Ugandan officials, and arranged a fraudulent Polish adoption. One employee pleaded guilty in 2019; others were charged in 2020.
nets.cite: US DOJ, 17 August 2020; The Guardian, 18 August 2020

nets.d: Baptist group whose ten members were arrested on 29 January 2010 taking 33 Haitian children to the Dominican Republic; leader Laura Silsby was convicted of arranging irregular travel.
French charity whose six members were convicted in Chad in December 2007 for trying to fly 103 children, falsely presented as Darfur orphans, to French host families.

nets.n: Nigerian 'baby factories' (recurring pattern, not a single organisation)
nets.reach_note: Makinde et al. list high incidence in Ondo, Ogun, Imo, Akwa Ibom, Abia and Anambra.
nets.d: Facilities posing as maternity homes, clinics or orphanages where pregnant girls and women are held (some raped) and their babies sold, including for illegal adoption. Raids: Enugu 2008, Aba 2011 (32 girls), Ihiala 2011, Imo 2013, Lagos 2018 (162 children).
nets.cite: Makinde et al., Trauma, Violence & Abuse (2015); BBC 26 April 2018; The Guardian 2 June 2011

nets.n: Pro Juventute 'Hilfswerk für die Kinder der Landstrasse'
nets.d: Programme of the Swiss foundation Pro Juventute, backed by federal authorities, that removed about 590 Yenish children from their families; recognised by the Swiss government as a crime against humanity in February 2025.

- Denmark: DIA closure (2024) and Danish government investigation of Korean adoptions. AP only says 'Denmark's only international adoption agency said it was shutting down'. No exact date.
- Belgium (no source opened), Mali 2009 and France's 2023 inspection details. Brandeis says only that Congo-Brazzaville, Mali and Madagascar temporarily shut adoptions after trafficking scandals, with no dates, so these were not added to closures.

- Nepal: the US Aug 2010 suspension of 'abandoned child' adoptions is only given in Wikipedia without a date, so it is not in closures. The halt by Nepal itself in 2007 is included.
- Cambodia: the Hague-related 2009 moratorium is not verified.
- Kenya: no official action was found after the BBC 2020 investigation.
- Nigeria: Enugu 2008 and Ihiala 2011 raids are in the net description only (AFP sources not opened).
- Egypt 2012, Gwalior India and Paraguay early-1990s trade: sources not opened.

- Ukraine: adoption into Russian families is recorded separately from deportations (conflict agent). There is no adoption-specific count.
- Russia/US 2012 ban is recorded as a closure. It is not a trafficking finding.
- The Korea flow by receiving country (MOHW 1953–2008) totals 163,898. The TRC uses 'more than 140,000', BBC 'at least 170,000' and AP 'about 200,000'. These estimates differ, and all are cited where used.
